issues.explanation: 'Noticing Weapons' is a poor fit for the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is evidence of weapon-related assault or generalized violence cues; the rest of the profile centers on interpersonal abuse and nonspecific danger rather than weapon-focused threat monitoring, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma context.

'Inaction Guilt' is clinically questionable in this context because it implies self-blame for not doing more to stop the abuse, which is less coherent with an ongoing coercive partner-abuse formulation than appraisals centered on shame, powerlessness, betrayal, or worthlessness. It is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it stands out as weakly aligned with the trauma narrative and node pattern.

vignette:
Anh Tran is a 51-year-old tax inspector who has been married for twenty-three years. Four years ago, his wife, in a fit of rage during an argument about their teenage son's school performance, struck him repeatedly across the face and chest with a metal cooking spoon. He had frozen, too stunned to defend himself, and the beating had continued until their son intervened. In the months that followed, Anh found himself unable to recall the exact sequence of that night-the memory arrived only in sudden, fragmentary flashes: the glint of the spoon, the sound of his own gasping, the look of contempt on his wife's face. He could not remember how he had ended up on the kitchen floor or what had been said afterward.

These fragments forced their way into his mind without warning, often when he was simply sitting at his desk reviewing tax returns. The unpredictability of these intrusions made him feel like an object, a thing that things happened to, rather than a person who could act. He had come to believe that nothing good could happen to him anymore, that he had been betrayed by the one person who was supposed to protect him. This sense of betrayal and dehumanization made him feel constantly on edge; he began to react as if he were in danger even when nothing was actually wrong, jumping at the sound of a colleague's footsteps.

The discomfort of feeling trapped in his own home-where his wife's voice, her presence in the next room, could trigger the memory fragments-meant that Anh started to feel unsafe unless his back was against a wall where he could see the room. At work, he began frequently looking behind him to check if someone was following him, a habit his colleagues noticed but did not comment on. The exhaustion of this constant vigilance made him feel very tired, and that fatigue itself became a trigger: when he was tired, the memory fragments came more easily, and his negative appraisals-that he was nothing, that he had been betrayed-felt more true.

He had come to believe that his own exhaustion was a sign that he was failing, that he was weak, and this belief made the unpredictability of his life feel even more threatening. The more he felt like an object, the more he avoided unpredictable situations-he stopped attending his son's basketball games, stopped visiting his own family on weekends, stopped going to the grocery store unless it was at a precise time when he knew it would be empty. At work, he took on only the most routine audits, refusing any case that required negotiating with taxpayers in person, because he could not tolerate the unpredictability of what they might say.

The memory fragments would surface most powerfully when he was tired, and the memory itself-the betrayal, the helplessness-reinforced his sense of being an object. This made him check behind him more often, made him feel unsafe in his own kitchen. He had started sleeping in the guest room, with a chair wedged under the doorknob, though he could not explain why that helped. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at his desk last month: he had been reviewing a routine audit, felt a wave of exhaustion, and then found himself on the floor, his hands over his head, with no memory of how he had gotten there. His supervisor had found him and suggested he take leave. Anh is afraid that if he does not get control of this, he will lose his job, but what frightens him most is the thought that his wife might be right-that he is, after all, just an object, and objects do not deserve to feel safe.
